idiom_name: sqlx Pool::begin() Transaction + outbox row + relay
implementation_notes: The async database path is library-provided and safe by construction: sqlx::Pool::begin() (or Connection::begin) returns a Transaction that commits with .commit() and rolls back on drop, so the unit of work is a scoped value; the outbox row is inserted in the same transaction and a relay (a sqlx polling task or a LISTEN/NOTIFY-driven task) publishes committed rows and marks them sent. This is the mainstream Rust answer when the business state lives in a database, because the language and its clients offer no coordinator that can span a database and a broker.
pitfalls: A Transaction rolls back when dropped, so an early `?` return silently discards the unit of work; make the commit explicit and check its result.
Transaction borrows the connection and is not freely shareable across tasks: keep the unit of work on one task and pass data, not the transaction, to spawned tasks.
Reading the row from a second connection before the commit shows nothing, which is easy to misread as a write failure while the transaction is still open.

variants.name: rdkafka transactional producer
variants.implementation_notes: The broker-side realization through rust-rdkafka: after creating the producer you call init_transactions(), then begin_transaction(), send records (and send_offsets_to_transaction for consumed offsets), and finish with commit_transaction() or abort_transaction(); the crate is a safe wrapper over librdkafka and needs a librdkafka of a recent release. Use it for consume-transform-produce pipelines or when the business state lives in the cluster; it does not span a database, so a database-coupled service still writes an outbox row.
pitfalls: Only one transaction may be open per producer at a time, and the producer must not be shared across threads while a transaction is in flight.
The transactional id must be stable and unique per processor so the broker can fence zombies; a random id disables that protection.
Sends inside a transaction are not visible to consumers that read uncommitted data, so consumer configuration is part of the design.
